title: Eli Wilner November Frame Funding Program
summary: Eli Wilner & Company has announced that all funding allocated through its museum grant program for October 2026 has been fully committed in support of reframing and frame restoration projects at museums and cultural institutions nationwide. In response to continued demand, Eli Wilner & Company funding partners have committed an additional $125,000 for the November 2026 funding cycle. These funds will be awarded on a first-come, first-served basis through November 30, 2026, or until fully committed. The grants are intended to offset a portion of the cost of qualifying frame restoration and reframing projects. Recipient institutions are required to participate in the cost of the project, while grant funding covers the remaining approved portion. This shared-cost approach enables museums to undertake important projects that might otherwise be postponed due to budget limitations. New applications are currently being accepted via email

title: One of the earliest landscapes in Western art history to make auction debut
summary: Albrecht Altdorfer is widely considered the first landscape painter in the modern sense. Unlike contemporaries who only used nature as a backdrop for their religious or mythological figures, for Altdorfer the forest was also a rich subject in its own right. "The first independent landscapes in the history of European art were painted by Albrecht Altdorfer" -- Professor Christopher Wood, Academic & Scholar of Altdorfer¹ Until the discovery of this painting earlier this year, only two pure landscape oil paintings by him were known: one in the National Gallery in London and one in the Alte Pinakothek in Munich. The appearance of this thickly wooded landscape, densely painted on a parchment measuring some 23 by 20 centimetres, marks a historic moment. title: Meg Onli and Zack Winokur to co-organize the 2028 Whitney Biennial
summary: The Whitney Museum of American Art announces that Meg Onli, the Museum’s Nancy and Fred Poses Curator, and acclaimed director Zack Winokur will co-organize Whitney Biennial 2028. Bringing together two visionary artistic leaders whose practices span contemporary visual art, performance, music, and interdisciplinary collaboration, Onli and Winokur will lead the development of the eighty-third edition of the Museum’s landmark exhibition series, set to open in March 2028. Onli, who co-organized Whitney Biennial 2024: Even Better Than the Real Thing, is currently co-curator of the Whitney’s blockbuster exhibition Roy Lichtenstein: Like New, on view through May 10, 2027, the first full-scale retrospective of the artist’s work in New York City in more than three decades. Winokur is an internationally recognized director, the Co-Founder of AMOC* (American Modern Opera Company), and the former Artistic Director of Little Island. title: Long-lost Georgia O'Keeffe painting discovered in a Manhattan closet heads to Christie's
summary: “Oh, by the way, there's a Georgia O'Keeffe in the closet.” Those words—casually uttered recently by an “extremely private” and “incredibly accomplished” woman to a relative in her Manhattan apartment—led to the rediscovery of a long-lost Georgia O'Keeffe landscape that will now be seen publicly for the first time in at least three decades. Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I (in the region of $3 million), a 1930 O'Keeffe painting depicting the New Mexico landscape that would occupy her artistic imagination for the rest of her storied career, will be presented as part of Christie's 20th Century Evening Sale in New York on November 17. The work will be a highlight of Christie's New York Marquee Week, which includes the collections of Clive Davis, Herbert Lust, Antonio Homem Sonnabend, and others. title: Hauser & Wirth opens first New York solo exhibition of new works by Spanish artist Cristina Iglesias
summary: For 'Possible Matter,' her first New York exhibition with Hauser & Wirth, Spanish artist Cristina Iglesias debuts a new immersive dome installation alongside four wall-based sculptures from her new 'Possible Matter' series, exploring the shifting boundaries between the built and natural worlds. With this exhibition, Iglesias brings two strands of an extraordinary practice into captivating dialogue, moving between expansion and erosion, formation and dissolution, the exhibition considers the interplay between natural processes and human invention. At the center of the exhibition is 'Dome' (2026), Iglesias's newest immersive work, following 'Aurora Borealis Star Dome' (2026), a major public commission she recently completed for the Princess Estelle Sculpture Park in Stockholm, Sweden. title: Ancient human remains discovered beneath Mexico City railway project reveal possible pre-Hispanic ossuary
summary: Archaeologists working along the route of the Mexico City–Querétaro passenger railway have uncovered a possible ancient ossuary containing human remains, ceramics and stone artifacts near the Buenavista terminal, in a discovery that could shed new light on burial practices during one of the most transformative periods in Mexican history. The discovery, announced by Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), includes nine sets of human skeletal remains, five mandibles and a variety of other bones, some of which show evidence of intentional cranial modification. Associated objects suggest that the deposit may date to the Late Postclassic period (1200–1519 CE) or the early years of contact between Indigenous communities and Spanish conquerors (1519–1535 CE). title: Esther Schipper, Berlin opens an exhibition by Jenny Brosinski with all new paintings
summary: Jenny Brosinski’s paintings are cool, serious, and at times funny, but also fragile and moving. How can all of this be true at the same time? This is why the artist chose to be a painter: The medium allows her to accommodate these different qualities in a single work. The surface holds several decisions taken over time, giving them a silent stage. The individual steps that make up the painting – a circle of blue, an apparition in white, a cross in red – are clearly visible; you can trace every move. There is no attempt to take away what has been done. There is hardly any painting, you would almost say, considering the limited amount of elements that form the composition and the generous space around the motifs. There is a constellation of lines, and colors. In this theater of reduction, each step carries the weight of a main act. title: David Nolan Gallery opens third exhibition of rubber-tire sculptures and mixed media by Chakaia Booker
summary: David Nolan Gallery is presenting Unpacked, Chakaia Booker's third solo exhibition with the gallery. At the gallery's new location in Tribeca, we turn to the full breadth of media Booker has mastered, alongside the rubber-tire sculptures for which she is best known. The exhibition brings together freestanding and wall sculpture, from the intimate to the monumental; multilayered collaged works on paper, a practice she has maintained since 2009; a tapestry born of one such work; and a series of photographs that invite the viewer to see what the artist has seen. For more than four decades, Booker has cut and contorted rubber tires into abstract form, a practice that began in the 1980s, when she first took note of tires abandoned after street fires around the city. title: Australia's most significant new museum opens in Sydney
summary: Powerhouse Parramatta, one of the world’s most significant new cultural projects, will open in late 2026. Located on the banks of the Parramatta River, the future-focused museum will be a major new landmark for Australia and a global cultural destination for Western Sydney. The museum is the largest cultural infrastructure project in Australia since the Sydney Opera House, at 30,000 sqm designed by Franco-Japanese architects Moreau Kusunoki (Lead Designer) and Australian architecture firm Genton (Local Architect). The transformational project is the first state cultural institution to be built in Western Sydney, one of Australia’s fastest growing and most diverse regions. Construction began over four years ago and the main building by delivery partner Lendlease is now complete, with interior exhibition fit outs underway across the site and final works continuing on the public domain.

summary: Juliens’ Auctions announces Bold Luxury: “As Seen On” Edit, an auction featuring a curated collection of screen-worn and archival fashion from the wardrobe of Meryl Streep as Miranda Priestly in The Devil Wears Prada, bold styles worn by the characters of Emily in Paris, and other pieces from beloved fashion-forward TV shows and films. title: New V&A exhibition unites Byzantine and Ottoman artistic traditions for the first time in the UK
summary: Today, the V&A opens Constantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two Empires, a major exhibition that explores 1,600 years of extraordinary artistic production in one of the world’s most influential cities. Spanning AD 330 to 1922, it brings together remarkable works of art, design and architecture to reveal the enduring creative legacy of an imperial capital that shaped the Mediterranean world and far beyond. The first exhibition in the UK to tell this story in full, it offers a compelling new perspective on a city defined by artistic excellence across more than a millennium. The city once called Constantinople and now called Istanbul was the imperial and religious capital at the heart of two successive empires: the Byzantine (AD 330–1453) and the Ottoman (1453–1922), and the exhibition explores their distinct yet connected traditions of art and design, built across sixteen centuries. title: BUDDS and Weatherbys to auction 591 lots of horse racing history at the National Horse Racing Museum
summary: Two items in this BUDDS sale show just how dangerous a sport horse racing can be. Lester Piggott narrowly escaped death during a horrific starting stalls accident at Epsom Racecourse aboard a horse named Winsor Boy. Winsor Boy panicked inside the starting stalls and forcefully ducked down and lunged forward, dragging Piggott through a narrow gap at the bottom framework of the gate. The saddle Lester used that day is for sale. Green paint from the stalls is still on the underside, and Piggott later signed it. (Lot 60; £2,000–£3,000). A second near miss took place at the start of the 1993 Grand National when the starting tapes struck Richard Dunwoody's undershirt and tore at the collar where the starting tape caught round his neck. The shirt is in the sale as (Lot 119; £1,000–£1,500). After two false starts, 30 of the 39 runners set off anyway, and the race was declared void. title: Château Mouton Rothschild and Sotheby's to present landmark centenary auction
summary: On 4 February 2027, Sotheby's will present Château Mouton Rothschild: Paintings for the Labels — 100th Anniversary Commemorative Release, a landmark auction drawn directly from the château's cellars celebrating 100 years of the pioneering artist-label tradition begun by Jean Carlu in 1924. The sale will include both the inaugural 1924 vintage and the 2024 vintage, whose artist-label will be unveiled on 1 December 2026. Marking a milestone in the history of the artist labels, a tradition carried forward by three generations of the family and now one of the defining expressions of Mouton Rothschild's identity, the sale brings together historic vintages, a limited number of previously unreleased large formats and commemorative lots, alongside a barrel of the 2025 vintage. title: Casey Kaplan showcases large-scale paintings, dreamlike figures, and fresco-like surfaces by Ella Walker
summary: For her third solo exhibition at Casey Kaplan, Ella Walker (b. 1993, Manchester, UK) presents The Street, a new body of work roused from a lucid dream of remembered places and human intrigue set halfway between the Renaissance and present day. Across six large scale paintings, a cast of characters move through brick-lined streets with uncanny spatial logic, fragmenting their bodies into a palimpsest of limbs, faces, and disembodied hands. Layered and diluted paint flows in translucent swathes of color dammed by assertive outlines, occasionally revealing the ghostly pentimenti of an altered pose or worked-over figure. Introducing contemporary costumes and observed environments, Walker’s expanded visual language grounds and reinvents the drama of an interior self set loose in the outside world. title: Flawless diamond and four Kashmir sapphires headline Heritage's Holiday Jewelry Auction
summary: Rarity takes many forms in Heritage’s Dec. 7 Holiday Fine Jewelry Signature® Auction: a technically perfect diamond, four Kashmir sapphires with no evidence of heating and a miniature polar landscape created in an edition of just 22. Together, these highlights anchor an auction that pairs exceptional gemstones with distinctive creations by some of jewelry’s most celebrated designers. “The word that defines this auction is rarity,” says Jill Burgum, Heritage’s Executive Director of Fine Jewelry. “A Flawless diamond is remarkable on its own. To offer it alongside four unheated Kashmir sapphires gives bidders several very different opportunities to find something truly special.” The 3.52-carat rectangular step-cut diamond at the center of a custom-made platinum and 18k gold ring brings that theme into sharp focus. title: Silverlens opens an exhibition of speculative basketball paintings and drawings by Jenifer K Wofford
summary: What if basketball had been invented by Filipinas, and they still ruled the court? That’s the premise of Empress, Jenifer K Wofford’s speculative origin myth for the game. In the intimate exhibition space, Wofford’s squad confronts you the moment you walk in. You are in their house, and amidst the skirmish. The women who live here are completely sovereign. Ruling, yet unruly. Wofford’s paintings world-build around a 1910s photograph of a girls’ team from Apalit, Pampanga. American colonizers brought the sport to the Philippines in the early 1900s as a sport for girls in the public school system. Then conservative Catholic groups had it struck from the curriculum, fearing that young women in bloomers would pick up aggression, promiscuity, even lesbianism. title: Walters Art Museum opens an exhibition exploring animal materials, artistry, and conservation
summary: On November 7, the Walters Art Museum opens Luxury & Loss: Feather, Shell, Tusk, Horn, a major exhibition that explores luxurious art objects crafted from four natural materials taken from the animal world: kingfisher feather, tortoiseshell, elephant ivory, and rhinoceros horn. For centuries, these materials were prized by the powerful and wealthy for their beauty, scarcity, and the skill required to obtain and work with them. The exhibition will also examine the evolving understanding of how the consumption of materials from these animals over centuries contributed to the eventual decline and endangerment of their respective wild animal populations, which resulted in governments worldwide banning the commercial trade of all four materials in the 20th century. summary: This fall, Kay WalkingStick / Hudson River School, opens at The James Museum on November 7 at the start of National Native American Month. Developed by The New York Historical, the exhibition showcases landscape paintings by the renowned contemporary Cherokee artist Kay WalkingStick in conversation with classic works from The New York Historical’s collection of 19th-century Hudson River School paintings including work by the illustrious painter Albert Bierstadt. This stunning exhibition is the result of a close collaboration between the artist and Wendy Nālani E. title: kaufmann repetto presents fourth solo exhibition of new works by artist Dianna Molzan
summary: kaufmann repetto is presenting Dianna Molzan’s fourth solo exhibition at the gallery, Bio Casino. The exhibition draws on the fundamental desire for humans to create, tinker, and transform. As a species, our innovations brought about by this intrinsic trait have subsequently impact the natural world and our ever-shifting way of life. Molzan’s works subtly reference historic inventions that have shaped our modern surroundings. Through formal qualities such as pattern, color, and material, Molzan’s works take inspiration from patchworked agricultural fields, ancient systems of water distribution like fountains and pipes, and the transfiguration of raw materials into technological objects such as glass beads. title: New Orleans Museum of Art opens solo exhibition of works by contemporary painter Danielle Mckinney
summary: The New Orleans Museum of Art opened a survey of paintings by the American artist Danielle Mckinney. Titled Danielle Mckinney: Shelter, the exhibition includes over 40 paintings and works on paper spanning the last five years of the artist’s practice, marking her most comprehensive museum exhibition to date. McKinney was just selected as part of the TIME100 Inaugural Art class, comprised of leaders shaping the future of the field. Danielle Mckinney: Shelter will be on view at NOMA starting November 6, 2026, through summer 2027. “Mckinney’s paintings are profound reflections of intimate moments captured in rich painting techniques of oil and acrylic. title: Pace presents New York solo exhibition of new paintings by Li Hei Di
summary: Pace presents the year of mud, an exhibition of new paintings by London-based artist Li Hei Di, at its 540 West 25th Street gallery from November 6 through December 19. Marking the artist’s first solo exhibition with Pace in New York since they joined the gallery’s program in 2024, the year of mud situates Li’s oneiric, effervescent compositions in a mediated viewing environment. Existing between figuration and abstraction, Li’s paintings inhabit a space where certainty begins to dissolve. Li understands life as an ongoing act of transformation—an unending negotiation between interior experience and external reality. Their figures are never fixed, continually shifting between states of becoming and allowing the body to function less as a stable form than as a vessel through which memory, emotion, and desire flow. title: Sprüth Magers presents first UK solo exhibition of new and earlier paintings by Hyun-Sook Song
summary: Painting, for Hyun-Sook Song, is an analogue refuge. Transplanted from an early life in mid-century rural South Korea to the workforce in a rapidly modernising West Germany, Song turned to art-making to image fragmentary memories of a past life and, through them, a fading cultural paradigm. The forms she delineates with only a few sweeping brushstrokes carry the material and muscle memories of the cyclical agriculture that sustained life in the mountain village where she was born – harvesting rice with a sickle, uncoiling threads from silk cocoons. Song builds her canvases through a carefully choreographed sequence of movements, akin to the breath-guided flow of qigong, to channel invisible forces as she applies the egg tempera paint.
